s-11-steps.alt: The six steps, with what happens at each. 1, Filed: A legislator files the bill, and it goes to a committee. 2, Hearing: The committee holds a hearing and takes testimony on the bill. Many state legislatures take testimony from the public there. In Congress, the committee hears the witnesses it invites. A bill’s own page says how to take part. 3, Committee vote: The committee votes on whether to send the bill to the full House or Senate. 4, First chamber: The full House or Senate, wherever the bill was filed, votes on it. 5, Second chamber: The other chamber takes the bill up. Its own committee can hold a hearing first, and then the full chamber votes and both chambers agree on one text. Nebraska has one chamber, so a Nebraska bill keeps this step under a slash. 6, Governor or President: The governor signs a state bill and the President signs a federal one. Either can veto it, and lawmakers can vote to override a veto.

s-12-owner-correct.alt: A frame titled Who owns the next step?, for a federal records request, in four numbered steps. Each step names who acts, what they do, and who owns the next step, with the deadline the law sets. Step 1: You. Send a written request that describes the records you want to the agency’s records office. Next step: The agency’s records office. Twenty working days to decide whether to release the records, from the day the request arrives. Step 2: The agency’s records office. Confirms the request with a tracking number, searches for the records, reviews them, blacking out what an exemption protects, and sends a written answer with the records it can release. Next step: You. At least 90 days to appeal a refusal or a partial answer. Step 3: You. If you appeal, write to the agency’s appeal office. Next step: The agency’s appeal office. Twenty working days to decide the appeal. Step 4: The agency’s appeal office. Reviews the answer and decides whether to release more. Next step: You, again. Ask the National Archives’ records ombudsman to mediate, or sue in federal court. Sources: 5 U.S.C. 552, the Freedom of Information Act, sections (a)(6)(A), (h)(3) and (a)(4)(B), as in force on November 9, 2026, via the Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School; and FOIA.gov, “Frequently Asked Questions”, Office of Information Policy, U.S. Department of Justice, no page date; both retrieved November 9, 2026. Federal agencies only; states set their own records laws.
s-12-owner-correct.notes: V4.2's frame ("Give every handoff an owner."), with the deadlines and routes from the research notes, section 7A (5 U.S.C. 552(a)(6)(A), (a)(6)(A)(ii), (h)(3), (a)(4)(B)).
